questions.sec: Chronic hepatitis · etiologies, progression and laboratory monitoring
questions.q: What are the most common (m/c) and second most common causes of chronic hepatitis in adults?
opts: Hepatitis B is most common, followed by Hepatitis C
Alcohol is most common, followed by Wilson's disease
Autoimmune hepatitis is most common, followed by Budd-Chiari syndrome
NASH is most common, followed by alcohol as second most common
questions.exp: Under causes of chronic hepatitis, NASH is tagged '(m/c)' and alcohol as '(2nd m/c)'. (Book p997)

questions.sec: Chronic hepatitis · etiologies, progression and laboratory monitoring
questions.q: Match each clinical age group with its characteristic etiologies of chronic hepatitis — 1) Pediatric age group causes 2) Adult secondary causes … A) Autoimmune disease, Wilson's disease, hemochromatosis, Budd-Chiari syndrome, and biliary cirrhosis B) Cholestasis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, and Indian childhood cirrhosis
questions.exp: In children, causes are cholestasis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, and Indian childhood cirrhosis; adult causes include autoimmune, Wilson's, hemochromatosis, Budd-Chiari, and biliary cirrhosis. (Book p997)

questions.sec: Chronic hepatitis · etiologies, progression and laboratory monitoring
questions.q: What is the expected life expectancy of a patient who enters decompensated cirrhosis without liver transplantation?
questions.exp: Under decompensation in the disease progression chart, the text notes: '(Life expectancy 2 years without transplant)'. (Book p997)

questions.sec: Chronic hepatitis · etiologies, progression and laboratory monitoring
questions.q: Fill up: As chronic hepatitis progresses toward established cirrhosis, physical examination and imaging typically reveal gross ______ of the liver.
questions.exp: Under cirrhosis in the progression flowchart, the text notes 'Shrinkage of liver seen'. (Book p997)

questions.sec: Chronic hepatitis · etiologies, progression and laboratory monitoring
questions.q: What is the most common (m/c) constitutional symptom signalling disease progression in chronic hepatitis?
questions.exp: Under progression features, fatigue is explicitly annotated with '(m/c)'. (Book p997)

questions.sec: Chronic hepatitis · etiologies, progression and laboratory monitoring
questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a clinical symptom indicating progression of chronic hepatitis?
questions.exp: Features of progression listed are Fatigue (m/c), Altered sleep rhythm, Muscle wasting, Loss of libido, and Hepatomegaly; fever is not among them. (Book p997)

questions.sec: Chronic hepatitis · etiologies, progression and laboratory monitoring
questions.q: During routine clinical examination of a patient with suspected progressive chronic hepatitis, hepatomegaly is palpated. What is the indicated quantitative test to ascertain the degree of fibrosis?
questions.exp: The flowchart notes that if hepatomegaly is seen: 'Fibroscan : Quantitative test to ascertain degree of fibrosis'. (Book p997)

questions.sec: Chronic hepatitis · etiologies, progression and laboratory monitoring
questions.q: What laboratory transaminase pattern and numerical ceiling are typical of uncomplicated chronic hepatitis?
opts: ALT/AST elevation < 150 U/L with ALT > AST
ALT/AST elevation > 1000 U/L with AST > ALT
questions.exp: Under laboratory investigation for chronic hepatitis, the line reads: 'ALT/AST ↑ (<150 U/L) with ALT > AST'. (Book p997)

questions.sec: Chronic hepatitis · etiologies, progression and laboratory monitoring
questions.q: Assess the two statements on chronic hepatitis: I Patients with chronic hepatitis are usually asymptomatic and frequently detected on routine screening with LFTs. II Once cirrhosis develops, the three major life-threatening pathways are portal hypertension, hepatocellular carcinoma, and liver failure.
questions.exp: Both statements are true: chronic hepatitis is usually asymptomatic and found on LFT screening, and cirrhosis leads to portal HTN, HCC, and liver failure. (Book p997)

questions.sec: Chronic hepatitis · etiologies, progression and laboratory monitoring
questions.q: A 44-year-old man with obesity and dyslipidemia undergoes a health checkup. He feels mildly fatigued but has no jaundice or ascites. LFTs show ALT 82 U/L and AST 54 U/L (both <150 U/L, ALT > AST). What is the primary management strategy for his liver enzyme monitoring?
opts: Initiation of intravenous high-dose N-acetylcysteine therapy
Continuous monitoring of liver enzymes along with evaluation for NASH
Immediate emergency referral for orthotopic liver transplantation
questions.exp: The management section highlights 'Continuous monitoring of liver enzymes' and screening for treatable causes such as NASH. (Book p997)

questions.sec: Chronic hepatitis · etiologies, progression and laboratory monitoring
questions.q: Fill up: In children, chronic hepatitis progressing to early cirrhosis may be caused by ______ deficiency or Indian childhood cirrhosis.
questions.exp: Pediatric causes listed include cholestasis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, and Indian childhood cirrhosis. (Book p997)

questions.sec: Screening, early therapy, cirrhosis pathology and fibrosis staging
questions.q: Which of the following conditions is NOT listed under routine screening for chronic hepatitis on this page?
opts: Autoimmune hepatitis, Wilson's disease, and Hemochromatosis
questions.exp: Routine screening covers NASH, HBV/HCV, Autoimmune hepatitis, Wilson's disease, and Hemochromatosis. (Book p998)

questions.sec: Screening, early therapy, cirrhosis pathology and fibrosis staging
questions.q: Match each cause of chronic liver disease with the early intervention that yields very good therapeutic outcomes — 1) Hemochromatosis 2) Wilson's disease 3) NASH … A) Early penicillamine therapy B) Weight loss C) Early phlebotomy
questions.exp: Treatment before/during progression yields good outcomes with early phlebotomy for hemochromatosis, early penicillamine for Wilson's, and weight loss for NASH. (Book p998)

questions.sec: Screening, early therapy, cirrhosis pathology and fibrosis staging
questions.q: What is the defining pathological definition of cirrhosis?
opts: Centrilobular hemorrhagic necrosis without architectural remodeling
Microvesicular steatosis confined to zone 3 hepatocytes
Isolated granulomatous destruction of interlobular bile ducts
Normal lobular architecture lost and replaced by nodules connected by fibrous septation
questions.exp: Cirrhosis is defined as: 'Normal lobular architecture of liver lost and replaced by nodules connected by fibrous septation.' (Book p998)

questions.sec: Screening, early therapy, cirrhosis pathology and fibrosis staging
questions.q: Fill up: On gross surgical and post-mortem inspection, a cirrhotic liver characteristically presents with a ______ colour, irregular surface, and nodular texture.
questions.exp: The specimen caption describes: 'Cirrhotic liver lives with tawny brown colour irregular surface and nodular texture'. (Book p998)

questions.sec: Screening, early therapy, cirrhosis pathology and fibrosis staging
questions.q: What microscopic feature distinguishes a cirrhotic liver from normal hepatic parenchyma?
opts: Pure portal triad inflammation without any stromal septa
Complete absence of biliary ductules and endothelial fenestrations
Disorganised architecture with regenerative nodules surrounded by fibrous septa
Preserved hexaconal lobules radiating from central veins
questions.exp: Microscopy shows 'Disorganised architecture with regenerative nodule surrounded by fibrous septa'. (Book p998)

questions.sec: Screening, early therapy, cirrhosis pathology and fibrosis staging
questions.q: Match each stage of hepatic fibrosis with its histopathological definition — 1) Stage 1 2) Stage 2 3) Stage 3 4) Stage 4 … A) 2+ Bridging fibrosis extending to the next portal tract B) 3+ Nodules representing full-blown cirrhosis C) Mild periportal fibrosis D) 1+ Septation
questions.exp: The staging runs: Stage 1 = mild periportal fibrosis, Stage 2 = 1+ septation, Stage 3 = 2+ bridging fibrosis extending to next portal tract, and Stage 4 = 3+ nodules (full-blown cirrhosis). (Book p998)

questions.sec: Screening, early therapy, cirrhosis pathology and fibrosis staging
questions.q: Fill up: In the staging of hepatic fibrosis, Stage 3 is characterised by ______ fibrosis extending across to the next portal tract.
questions.exp: Stage 3 is defined as '2+ Bridging fibrosis : Fibrosis extending to next portal tract'. (Book p998)

questions.sec: Screening, early therapy, cirrhosis pathology and fibrosis staging
questions.q: Assess the two statements on hepatic fibrosis staging: I Stage 2 fibrosis is defined by 1+ septation without complete architectural nodularity. II Stage 4 represents full-blown cirrhosis characterized by regenerative nodules surrounded by fibrous septa.
questions.exp: Both statements are true: Stage 2 has 1+ septation, and Stage 4 has 3+ nodules defining full-blown cirrhosis. (Book p998)

questions.sec: Screening, early therapy, cirrhosis pathology and fibrosis staging
questions.q: A liver biopsy specimen from a 49-year-old patient with chronic Hepatitis C demonstrates fibrous bands extending from one portal triad to an adjacent portal tract, but without complete regenerative nodule formation. What fibrosis stage is present?
questions.exp: Fibrosis extending to the next portal tract without nodules is Stage 3 (2+ bridging fibrosis). (Book p998)

questions.sec: Screening, early therapy, cirrhosis pathology and fibrosis staging
questions.q: Which intervention is specifically noted on this page to achieve a good outcome when instituted early in NASH?
questions.exp: Under treatment during progression, NASH is paired with 'weight loss -> Good outcome'. (Book p998)

questions.sec: Portal hypertension pathophysiology and liver failure signs
questions.q: Match each contributor to increased sinusoidal resistance in portal hypertension with its mechanism — 1) Mechanical cause 2) Functional cause … A) Decreased intrasinusoidal nitric oxide (NO) leading to vasoconstriction and defenestration B) Physical compression of sinusoidal channels by regenerating nodules
questions.exp: The mechanical cause is compression by nodules; the functional cause is decreased intrasinusoidal NO causing sinusoidal vasoconstriction and defenestration. (Book p999)

questions.sec: Portal hypertension pathophysiology and liver failure signs
questions.q: What is the primary compensatory mechanism triggered by elevated portal venous pressure?
opts: Selective spasm of the superior mesenteric artery
Upregulation of renal medullary aquaporin channels
Decompression via the formation of portosystemic collaterals
questions.exp: Increased portal venous pressure triggers the compensatory mechanism: 'Decompression, formation of collaterals'. (Book p999)

questions.sec: Portal hypertension pathophysiology and liver failure signs
questions.q: Assess the two statements on nitric oxide (NO) in cirrhosis: I Intrasinusoidal NO is decreased, driving sinusoidal vasoconstriction and defenestration. II Systemic NO is increased, inducing widespread splanchnic vasodilation and hyperdynamic circulation.
questions.exp: Both statements are true: cirrhosis features decreased intrasinusoidal NO (increased intrahepatic resistance) alongside increased systemic NO (splanchnic vasodilation). (Book p999)

questions.sec: Portal hypertension pathophysiology and liver failure signs
questions.q: Fill up: In portal hypertension pathophysiology, gut endotoxemia and increased systemic nitric oxide cause a profound loss in peripheral vascular resistance, driving a ______ circulation that elevates portal inflow.
questions.exp: The flowchart notes that loss in peripheral vascular resistance leads to 'Hyperdynamic circulation (↑ F)', where increased flow increases pressure. (Book p999)

questions.sec: Portal hypertension pathophysiology and liver failure signs
questions.q: How does splanchnic vasodilation stimulate neurohumoral volume retention in cirrhosis?
opts: Excessive degradation of vasopressin by the damaged liver
Decreased effective circulatory volume triggers the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and ADH
Direct mechanical stretching of atrial natriuretic peptide receptors
Suppression of central sympathetic adrenergic outflow
questions.exp: Widespread splanchnic vasodilation reduces effective circulatory volume, stimulating RAAS and ADH to expand intravascular volume and exacerbate the hyperdynamic state. (Book p999)

questions.sec: Portal hypertension pathophysiology and liver failure signs
questions.q: Match each early manifestation of elevated splenic vein pressure with its clinical milestone — 1) Splenomegaly (hypersplenism) 2) Thrombocytopenia … A) First biochemical finding (due to platelet trapping in the spleen) B) First clinical finding
questions.exp: Elevated splenic vein pressure causes splenomegaly as the 'First clinical finding' and thrombocytopenia (due to platelet trapping) as the 'First biochemical finding'. (Book p999)

questions.sec: Portal hypertension pathophysiology and liver failure signs
questions.q: A 52-year-old man with compensated cirrhosis presents for routine follow-up. He has a palpably enlarged spleen. Complete blood count shows platelets 78,000/µL. What is the mechanism behind this initial biochemical abnormality?
opts: Autoimmune destruction of platelets by anti-platelet GPIIb/IIIa antibodies
Direct toxic suppression of megakaryocytes by ethanol metabolites
Accelerated consumption of platelets inside coronary atherosclerotic plaques
Trapping and pooling of platelets in the congested spleen secondary to raised splenic vein pressure
questions.exp: Thrombocytopenia is the first biochemical finding, caused by the trapping of platelets within the congested spleen. (Book p999)

questions.sec: Portal hypertension pathophysiology and liver failure signs
questions.q: Which of the following physical signs of liver failure is attributed specifically to the hyperdynamic circulation rather than alcohol consumption?
questions.exp: Palmar erythema and hyperpigmentation are features of the hyperdynamic circulation; alopecia, parotid swelling, and Dupuytren's contracture are associated with alcohol consumption. (Book p999)

questions.sec: Portal hypertension pathophysiology and liver failure signs
questions.q: Which triad of clinical signs is specifically grouped under 'Associated with Alcohol Consumption' on this page?
questions.exp: The alcohol-associated features are explicitly listed as: Alopecia, Parotid Swelling, and Dupuytren's contracture. (Book p999)

questions.sec: Portal hypertension pathophysiology and liver failure signs
questions.q: Assess the two statements on cirrhosis hemodynamics: I Increased portal venous pressure is driven by both increased intrahepatic vascular resistance and increased portal blood flow. II Intrasinusoidal defenestration in cirrhosis is caused by an excess of intrasinusoidal nitric oxide.
questions.exp: Statement I is true because P proportional to R x F. Statement II is false because defenestration and vasoconstriction are caused by decreased intrasinusoidal NO. (Book p999)

questions.sec: Endocrine changes, collaterals and decompensated cirrhosis
questions.q: Why do male patients with advanced liver failure develop gynecomastia and testicular atrophy?
opts: Downregulation of peripheral estrogen receptors by hyperammonemia
Loss of hepatic 5-alpha reductase activity impairs conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT)
Direct hyperprolactinemia resulting from portal-systemic dopamine clearance
questions.exp: The page states: 'No 5-a Reductase : NO DHT (Dihydrotestosteron) -> Gynecomastia, Testicular atrophy.' (Book p1000)

questions.sec: Endocrine changes, collaterals and decompensated cirrhosis
questions.q: Fill up: In female patients with liver failure, a decrease in ______ contributes to peripheral hypoestrogenism.
questions.exp: The text notes: 'Decrease sex hormone binding globulins -> Hypoestrogenism in females.' (Book p1000)

questions.sec: Endocrine changes, collaterals and decompensated cirrhosis
questions.q: What is the direction of venous blood flow in the abdominal wall collaterals forming caput medusae?
opts: Flow directed towards the umbilicus from all directions
Flow directed downwards towards the groin in all abdominal veins
Flow directed radially away from the umbilicus
Flow directed upwards from the pubis toward the umbilicus only
questions.exp: The text explicitly specifies: 'Caput medusae (flow away from umbilicus)'. (Book p1000)

questions.sec: Endocrine changes, collaterals and decompensated cirrhosis
questions.q: Assess the two statements on cirrhosis decompensation: I The onset of overt jaundice in cirrhosis signifies hepatic failure and marks the onset of decompensation. II Caput medusae exhibits collateral venous flow traveling toward the umbilicus.
questions.exp: Statement I is true because jaundice is annotated as 'Sign of liver failure -> Decompensation'. Statement II is false because flow in caput medusae is away from the umbilicus. (Book p1000)

questions.sec: Endocrine changes, collaterals and decompensated cirrhosis
questions.q: Which of the following triad of complications defines decompensated cirrhosis in the presence of fully developed portal hypertension?
questions.exp: Under DECOMPENSATION, the three defining complications linked to full developed portal HTN are Ascites, Encephalopathy, and Variceal bleed. (Book p1000)

questions.sec: Endocrine changes, collaterals and decompensated cirrhosis
questions.q: A 56-year-old man with long-standing cirrhosis is brought to the hospital with fresh hematemesis from esophageal varices. Examination reveals prominent periumbilical collateral veins with flow directed away from the umbilicus, jaundice, and bilateral gynecomastia. How is this patient's cirrhosis categorized?
questions.exp: Fully developed portal HTN complicated by variceal bleeding, ascites, or encephalopathy (plus jaundice) constitutes decompensated cirrhosis. (Book p1000)

questions.sec: Endocrine changes, collaterals and decompensated cirrhosis
questions.q: Match each physical finding of cirrhosis with its underlying pathophysiological mechanism — 1) Caput medusae 2) Gynecomastia and testicular atrophy 3) Female hypoestrogenism … A) Decreased sex hormone binding globulins B) Portal-systemic collateralization through recanalized umbilical veins with centrifugal flow C) Impaired 5-alpha reductase activity leading to lack of dihydrotestosterone
questions.exp: Caput medusae reflects collateral flow away from the umbilicus, lack of 5-alpha reductase drives lack of DHT (gynecomastia/atrophy), and decreased SHBG drives female hypoestrogenism. (Book p1000)

units.title: Chronic hepatitis etiologies, progression and laboratory monitoring
units.guide: NASH as most common and alcohol as second most common cause, pediatric etiologies (alpha-1 antitrypsin, Indian childhood cirrhosis), progression to cirrhosis and 2-year life expectancy in decompensation, fatigue as most common symptom, FibroScan indication for hepatomegaly, and ALT > AST (<150 U/L) transaminase monitoring.

units.title: Screening, early etiology-directed therapy and cirrhosis fibrosis staging
units.guide: Routine screening targets, early phlebotomy for hemochromatosis, penicillamine for Wilson's, weight loss for NASH, architectural loss replaced by nodules and fibrous septation, tawny brown appearance, and the 4-stage fibrosis scale (mild periportal, 1+ septation, 2+ bridging, 3+ nodules/cirrhosis).

units.title: Portal hypertension pathophysiology, hyperdynamic state and clinical stigmata
units.guide: Mechanical nodular compression versus functional decreased intrasinusoidal NO, systemic NO and gut endotoxemia driving hyperdynamic circulation, RAAS and ADH stimulation, splenomegaly as first clinical finding, thrombocytopenia as first biochemical finding, palmar erythema, and the alcohol-associated triad (alopecia, parotid swelling, Dupuytren's).

units.title: Endocrine disturbances, caput medusae and decompensated cirrhosis
units.guide: Absence of 5-alpha reductase causing lack of DHT with gynecomastia and testicular atrophy, decreased SHBG with female hypoestrogenism, caput medusae centrifugal flow, jaundice as decompensation herald, and the decompensation triad (ascites, encephalopathy, variceal bleed).
